Angular Async data & HTTP The resource API turns "fetch this, and tell me while it is loading" into three signals — and gets cancellation right, which hand-rolled versions rarely do. At a glance httpResource(url) for the common case; resource({ params, loader }) when the source is not HTTP; rxResource when the loader returns an Observable. All three expose value() , isLoading() , error() and status() as signals, plus reload() . The request is reactive : read a signal in it and it re-fetches when that signal changes, abandoning the previous result. HttpClient uses fetch by default from v22. Interceptors are functions, not classes. Angular Change detection & zoneless The most-misunderstood part of Angular, and the one where the last three versions changed the answer. At a glance Zoneless is the default for new applications from v21. provideZonelessChangeDetection() has been stable (without the Experimental prefix) since v20.2. OnPush is the default strategy from v22 — you no longer write changeDetection: at all. Under zoneless, mutating a plain field updates nothing . That is the single thing that breaks during migration. markForCheck() and detectChanges() still exist, and needing them is a signal that some state should be a signal. Try it Same tree, same event, three strategies. Watch how many components Angular visits — and pick "Zoneless" with a setTimeout to see the failure mode that catches everyone. What changed Note the two-step timeline: the API stabilised in v20.2, but v21 made it the default for new applications. An existing application upgraded to v21 or v22 keeps zone.js until you remove it — nothing is taken away from you on upgrade. How each strategy decides What schedules a pass What gets checked zone.js + Default Any patched async API: events, timers, XHR, promises Every component, every time zone.js + OnPush Same Components marked dirty — an event in the component, a changed input reference, an async pipe emission, a signal read in the template — plus their ancestors Zoneless A signal write, an async pipe emission, markForCheck() , or a template event handler Only the views that read the changed signal Migrating to zoneless The work is not the provider — it is finding the places that relied on zone.js noticing something. In rough order of how often they bite: 1. State mutated outside signals A field set in a setTimeout , a websocket callback, a third-party library's callback, or a promise .then() . Under zone.js all four triggered a pass. Under zoneless none of them do. Make the state a signal and the problem disappears at the source. 2. Array and object mutation this.items().

No changeDetection — OnPush is the default since v22. Dependencies come from imports on the component, not a module. Host bindings go in the host object, not @HostBinding / @HostListener decorators. DOM work goes in afterNextRender , not ngAfterViewInit . Do it this way now import { Component, input, output, computed, signal } from '@angular/core'; import { DatePipe } from '@angular/common'; @Component({ selector: 'user-card', imports: [DatePipe], host: { 'class': 'user-card', '[class.is-admin]': 'user().isAdmin', '(keydown.escape)': 'dismissed.emit()', }, template: ` {{ user().name }} Joined {{ user().joined | date }} @if (canEdit()) { <button (click)="edit()">Edit</button> } `, }) export class UserCard { user = input.required<User>(); readOnly = input(false); dismissed = output<void>(); edited = output<User>(); canEdit = computed(() => !this.readOnly() && this.user().isAdmin); edit() { this.edited.emit(this.user()); } } Nothing above is boilerplate you could remove. Compare it with the same component written for Angular 15 and roughly a third of the lines were ceremony. What changed Components written between v15 and v18 carry an explicit standalone: true . It still compiles — it is simply redundant now, and the ng generate @angular/core:standalone schematic will strip it along with any NgModules that existed only to declare components. This is the one v22 change that can alter runtime behaviour rather than just syntax. A component that mutated an object in place and relied on the old check-everything default to notice will stop updating. If that bites, the change-detection-eager schematic pins the old strategy explicitly so you can migrate component by component rather than all at once. Angular Dependency injection The most mechanical of the modern-Angular migrations, and the one that unlocked the rest: once inject() worked outside constructors, guards and interceptors could stop being classes. At a glance inject(Thing) as a field initialiser, not a constructor parameter. @Service() instead of @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) . provideAppInitializer() instead of the APP_INITIALIZER token. Guards, resolvers and interceptors are plain functions that call inject() . inject() only works in an injection context — that constraint is the one thing here worth understanding properly. Do it this way now import { Service, inject, InjectionToken } from '@angular/core'; import { HttpClient } from '@angular/common/http'; @Service() export class UserStore { private http = inject(HttpClient); private config = inject(APP_CONFIG); load(id: string) { return this.http.get<User>(`${this.config.apiUrl}/users/${id}`); } } // A token for anything that is not a class. export const APP_CONFIG = new InjectionToken<AppConfig>('APP_CONFIG', { providedIn: 'root', factory: () => ({ apiUrl: '/api' }), }); // Reusable logic that needs DI, without being a service. export function usePageTitle(title: string) { const titleService = inject(Title); titleService.setTitle(title); } What changed The reason this matters more than it looks: a constructor parameter can only be injected into a class being constructed. inject() works in any injection context, which is what makes a functional guard, a functional interceptor, or a shared useSomething() helper possible at all. @Injectable() is not deprecated and still works. @Service() is the shorter spelling of what almost every service wanted. Angular Modern Angular in one page If you last wrote Angular before v16, almost every idiom you know has a replacement. Here is the whole arc — what changed, in what order, and which parts you can ignore. The four shifts that matter NgModules became optional, then unnecessary. Components declare their own imports . Standalone is the default since v19; the standalone: true flag is now redundant. Signals replaced "tell Angular something changed". State that knows who reads it means Angular can update precisely what depends on it, instead of re-checking the tree. Structural directives became template syntax. @if , @for , @switch , @defer and @let are part of the language, not imports. Zone.js became optional. With signals carrying the change information, the library that patched every browser API to guess when to re-render is no longer needed. The arc, version by version Set the version you are on and the badges throughout this section will tell you what you already have: Version The headline What it meant in practice 14 Jun 2022 Standalone components (preview), typed forms inject() becomes broadly usable — the quiet change that later makes functional guards and interceptors possible. 15 Nov 2022 Standalone stable, functional router guards You could write a real application without a single NgModule. 16 May 2023 Signals (preview), takeUntilDestroyed , DestroyRef The reactivity rewrite starts. The destroy$ Subject pattern becomes obsolete. 17 Nov 2023 Built-in control flow, @defer , esbuild/Vite builder, angular.dev The biggest single break in template style since Angular 2. Builds get dramatically faster. 18 May 2024 Control flow and deferrable views stable; zoneless experimental @let arrives. Zoneless becomes something you can actually try. 19 Nov 2024 Standalone by default; linkedSignal and resource() in preview The standalone: true flag stops being needed. APP_INITIALIZER and friends are deprecated for provide* functions. 20 May 2025 Signals stabilise effect , linke

Angular Routing Guards became functions, lazy loading became per-component, and route parameters became inputs — so a routed component no longer needs to know the router exists. At a glance Guards and resolvers are plain functions. The class-based interfaces were removed in v16 — one of the few hard deadlines. loadComponent lazy-loads a single standalone component; loadChildren still loads a group of routes. withComponentInputBinding() binds route params, query params, data and resolved values to component inputs. Route config is a plain array — no RouterModule.forRoot . Do it this way now // app.routes.ts export const routes: Routes = [ { path: '', loadComponent: () => import('./home').then(m => m.Home) }, { path: 'users/:id', loadComponent: () => import('./user-detail').then(m => m.UserDetail), canActivate: [authGuard], resolve: { breadcrumb: breadcrumbResolver }, }, { path: 'admin', canMatch: [adminGuard], // skip the route entirely if it fails loadChildren: () => import('./admin/routes').then(m => m.adminRoutes), }, { path: '**', component: NotFound }, ]; // main.ts bootstrapApplication(App, { providers: [ provideRouter( routes, withComponentInputBinding(), withViewTransitions(), withInMemoryScrolling({ scrollPositionRestoration: 'enabled' }), ), ], }); What changed This one has a real deadline attached, unlike most of the changes in this reference: CanActivate and friends were deprecated in v15 and removed in v16 . Code still implementing those interfaces does not compile on any currently supported Angular version. The testing payoff is the real argument. A component that takes id as an input can be tested by setting an input. A component that reads ActivatedRoute needs the router harness, or a mock whose shape you have to get right. b: Angular Signals A value that knows who is reading it. That one property is what lets Angular update exactly what depends on a change — and what makes zoneless possible. The whole API signal(v) — writable state. Read with () , write with .set() or .update() . computed(fn) — derived, read-only, cached, lazy. effect(fn) — a side effect that re-runs when what it read changes. For talking to the outside world, not for deriving state. linkedSignal(…) — derived and writable: resets when its source changes, but can be overwritten in between. untracked(fn) — read without creating a dependency. pnpm How pnpm works Two design decisions — a shared content-addressable store and a non-flat node_modules — explain almost every way pnpm differs from npm, including the ones that look like bugs. At a glance One copy of each package version on disk globally, hard-linked into each project. Ten projects on the same version cost the space of one. node_modules contains only your declared dependencies . Everything else lives in node_modules/.pnpm and is symlinked. That is why an import you never declared stops resolving — a phantom dependency . It is the feature working. In v11 the store index is a single SQLite database rather than a file per package. The store npm downloads and extracts a copy of every package into every project. pnpm extracts each package version once , into a global content-addressable store keyed by hash, and builds each project's node_modules from hard links into it. The files are shared, so a second project using the same version costs essentially nothing. The practical consequences: installs are fast when the store is warm (nothing to download or extract), disk usage across many projects is a fraction of npm's, and offline installs work for anything you have installed before. Hard links mean edits are shared Editing a file inside node_modules to debug something edits the copy in the store, and therefore every project using that version. Use pnpm patch instead — it takes a copy, lets you edit it, and produces a patch file that is reapplied on install. The layout This is the part that changes behaviour rather than just performance. With npm's flat node_modules , every transitive dependency is hoisted to the top level, so require('lodash') works whether or not you declared lodash — as long as something in your tree depends on it. npm — flat and hoisted pnpm — only what you declared node_modules/ node_modules/ ├── express/ ├── express -> .pnpm/express@5.1.0/… ├── body-parser/ ← transitive └── .pnpm/ ├── cookie/ ← transitive ├── express@5.1.0/ ├── lod

At a glance pnpm-workspace.yaml lists the packages — and, since v11, holds all pnpm settings too. workspace:* means "the copy in this repo", and fails loudly if there isn't one. catalog: names a version once for the whole repo. --filter selects packages, including by dependency relationship and by what git says changed. The workspace file # pnpm-workspace.yaml packages: - 'apps/*' - 'libs/*' - '!**/dist/**' # One version per dependency, for the whole repo. catalog: typescript: ~7.0.2 rxjs: ^7.8.2 # Named catalogs, when one version genuinely is not enough. catalogs: angular22: '@angular/core': ^22.0.8 '@angular/common': ^22.0.8 '@angular/router': ^22.0.8 # v11: pnpm settings live here too, not in .npmrc allowBuilds: - esbuild - '@angular/build' // apps/web/package.json { "dependencies": { "@angular/core": "catalog:angular22", "@angular/common": "catalog:angular22", "rxjs": "catalog:", "@acme/ui": "workspace:*" } } Why catalogs matter for Angular Angular packages must move in lockstep — @angular/core at 22 with @angular/router at 21 fails at runtime in ways that are tedious to diagnose. In a monorepo with eight packages that each list eight Angular dependencies, that is 64 version strings to keep identical, and upgrading means editing all of them. With a catalog it is one block. Drift becomes impossible rather than merely discouraged, and the upgrade is a single edit. catalog: is rewritten on publish A published package cannot carry "catalog:" — consumers have no catalog. pnpm replaces it with the resolved version when packing, the same way it handles workspace: . This is only a concern for packages you actually publish. The workspace protocol Specifier Means Published as workspace:* The local package, any version The exact version workspace:^ The local package ^ plus the version workspace:~ The local package ~

A value that knows who is reading it. A container holding a value, read by calling it (count()). When the value changes, everything that read it is notified — so the framework knows exactly which views depend on which state, without diffing anything. This is the mechanism zoneless change detection is built on.

A signal derived from other signals, recalculated only when they change. A read-only signal defined by a function of other signals. It caches its value and recomputes lazily on first read after any dependency changes. Dependencies are tracked automatically by what the function actually reads on each run, so a branch not taken creates no dependency.

A side effect that re-runs when the signals it reads change. A function registered to run after any signal it read has changed. Effects are for synchronising with things outside the reactive graph — logging, the DOM, a third-party library. Deriving state inside an effect is almost always a computed() in disguise.

You never observe a half-updated state. A property of a reactive system: when several values derive from a common source, an observer never sees them briefly disagree. If a and b both derive from x, nothing runs between a updating and b updating. Angular's signal graph guarantees this; a naive listener-based system does not.

Angular without zone.js patching the browser to guess when to re-render. A change detection mode where Angular is told what changed by signals rather than inferring it. Historically zone.js monkey-patched setTimeout, addEventListener and friends so Angular could re-check the whole component tree after any of them fired. Zoneless removes that: less startup cost, smaller bundles, no patched globals, and change detection that runs only where something actually changed.

Angular working out which bindings in the template need re-rendering. The pass where Angular compares each template binding's current value against the last one it rendered and updates the DOM where they differ. What varies between strategies is not the comparison but which components get visited at all.

Only re-check this component when its inputs or signals actually change. A change detection strategy that skips a component unless one of its inputs changed by reference, an event fired inside it, a signal it reads changed, or it was explicitly marked. Since Angular 22 this is the default for components that do not set changeDetection.

An injectable handle for "when this thing is torn down". A token providing an onDestroy callback in any injection context — component, directive, service or function. It is what lets takeUntilDestroyed() work without a lifecycle hook.

Unsubscribe automatically when the surrounding thing is destroyed. An RxJS operator from @angular/core/rxjs-interop that completes a stream when the current injection context is destroyed. Replaces the manual destroy$ Subject plus ngOnDestroy pattern. Called outside an injection context it needs an explicit DestroyRef.

The moments when Angular knows which injector you belong to, so inject() works. The window during which inject() can resolve a dependency: field initialisers and constructors of injectables, factory functions, and callbacks run inside runInInjectionContext(). Calling inject() outside one — in a lifecycle hook, or inside a promise callback — throws.

A component that declares its own template dependencies instead of relying on a module. A component, directive or pipe carrying its own imports array. Introduced in preview in v14, stable in v15, the default since v19 — at which point the standalone: true flag became redundant. The NgModule it replaced existed only to tell the compiler what a template could see.

The old container that told the compiler which components a template could use. A decorator collecting declarations, imports, exports and providers. Every component had to be declared in exactly one. Standalone components made this indirection unnecessary; NgModules still work and still appear in older codebases, but nothing new needs them.

A chunk of template that is not downloaded until it is needed. A template block whose contents — and their dependencies — are split into a separate bundle and loaded on a trigger: on viewport, on interaction, on idle, on timer, or when a condition becomes true. The most direct lever Angular gives you over initial bundle size.

Making server-rendered HTML interactive without throwing it away and re-rendering. The client-side pass that attaches event listeners and reactive state to markup the server already produced. Without it, Angular would discard the server's DOM and rebuild it, causing a visible flicker and wasting the server work.

Hydrate parts of the page only when they are needed, not all at once. An extension of hydration that uses @defer triggers to decide when each block becomes interactive, so the JavaScript for a footer or a modal is neither downloaded nor executed until something asks for it. Event replay records interactions that happen before a block hydrates and applies them afterwards.

Rendering the first version of the page on the server. Server-side rendering: producing HTML on the server so the browser can paint before any application JavaScript runs. Improves perceived load time and is what search engines and link previews see.

An async load whose loading state, error and value are all signals. resource() and its HTTP-specific sibling httpResource() model an asynchronous fetch as a reactive unit: value(), isLoading() and error() are signals you read in a template, and the request re-runs when its reactive inputs change. Stable in Angular 22.

A stream of values over time that you subscribe to. The core RxJS type: a producer that pushes zero or more values to a subscriber, then either completes or errors. Unlike a Promise it can emit many times, is lazy (nothing happens until subscription), and is cancellable.

Does each subscriber get its own run, or do they share one? A cold Observable starts its work per subscriber — two subscribers to an HTTP call make two requests. A hot Observable produces independently of subscription and shares one run — subscribers see whatever is emitted while they are listening. Most surprises in RxJS trace back to this distinction.

An Observable you can push values into by hand. Both an Observable and an observer. Variants differ in what a late subscriber sees: Subject nothing, BehaviorSubject the current value, ReplaySubject the last n values, AsyncSubject only the final value on completion.

A picture of a stream as beads on a timeline. A notation for what an Observable emits and when: characters along a line, where each frame is a unit of virtual time, | is completion and # is an error. Also an executable test format — RxJS's TestScheduler runs marble strings directly.

Run time-based stream tests instantly, using virtual time. An RxJS scheduler that replaces real time with virtual frames, so a test of a five-second debounce finishes immediately and deterministically. Paired with marble syntax to assert what a stream emitted and exactly when.

What to do when a stream emits another stream. The family — switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, exhaustMap — that subscribes to an inner Observable produced per outer value. They differ only in what happens when a new outer value arrives while an inner is still running: switch cancels it, merge runs both, concat queues, exhaust ignores the new one.

Angular's test harness for building a component with real dependency injection. The API that configures a testing module, instantiates components and resolves their injectables, giving you a ComponentFixture to drive and inspect. The alternative — constructing the class directly — is faster but tests nothing about templates or DI.

A stable API for driving a component in a test, instead of poking at its DOM. A class exposing a component's behaviour as methods (click(), getText()) so tests do not depend on its internal markup. Introduced by the Angular CDK; the payoff is that a component's internal refactor does not break every test that touched it.

A code generator or codemod shipped with the framework. A packaged transformation run by the Angular CLI, either scaffolding new files or rewriting existing source. Migration schematics are the mechanism that makes Angular's breaking changes tractable — ng update runs the ones for the version you are stepping to.

Importing a package you never declared, which happens to be there anyway. Code that imports a package listed nowhere in its package.json but resolvable because a flat node_modules hoisted a transitive dependency to the top. It works until the dependency tree shifts. pnpm's non-flat layout makes it fail immediately instead, which is the point.

One copy of each package version on disk, shared by every project. pnpm's global store, keyed by content hash. A project's node_modules is built from hard links into it, so ten projects using the same version cost the space of one. As of pnpm 11 the store index is a single SQLite database rather than a file per package.

"I need this, but the app should supply it, and we must agree on the version." A dependency a package expects its consumer to provide, so both end up using the same instance — essential for anything with shared global state, which is why every Angular library peer-depends on @angular/core. pnpm is stricter about unmet peers than npm, which surfaces real version conflicts that were previously silent.

Name a dependency version once for the whole monorepo. A pnpm workspace feature: define versions in a catalog and have packages reference catalog: instead of a literal range. One edit updates every package, and drift between packages becomes impossible — which is what you want for a set like @angular/* that must move in lockstep.

"This dependency is the copy in this repo, not one from the registry." A pnpm version specifier (workspace:*, workspace:^) that resolves to a local package in the same workspace and fails loudly if there isn't one. On publish it is rewritten to a real version range.

The exact tree that was installed, written down so it can be reproduced. A generated file pinning every resolved version and integrity hash. Committing it is what makes an install reproducible; installing with --frozen-lockfile in CI is what proves nobody changed a dependency without changing the lockfile.
